The information we present today and our comments and answers to your questions reflect management's views as of today. Please refer to the latest safe harbor statement in our earnings release, which also applies to this call. The call will be conducted in Mandarin with simultaneous English interpretation provided by an external provider. In the event of any discrepancy, the Chinese remarks will prevail.

    Today's slides are available on our Investor Relations website. Now I'll turn the call over to Mr. Yu Li, our CEO and Executive Director, to review our third quarter 2026 results.

    Yu Li: Thank you. Hello, investors and analysts. I'm Yu Li, CEO and Executive Director of Super Hi International. Let me walk you through our operating performance for the third quarter of 2026. This quarter, we stayed with our long-term strategy of focusing on both employees and guests. We worked to improve the guest experience, refine our menu and manage each restaurant more closely. Haidilao restaurants served 8.4 million guest visits, up 3.7% year-over-year. Both overall and same-store average table turnover reached 4x per day, up 0.1 turn each. Haidilao restaurant revenue rose by 2.4%. We also continue to grow revenue beyond dine-in and advance our Pomegranate Proposal. Combined revenue from delivery and other businesses grew by 78.2% year-over-year.

    It has been revealed that that helped lift total revenue to $229 million, up 7.1% year-over-year and 4.8% quarter-over-quarter. Operating profit was $9.933 million with an operating margin of 4.3%. As we improved operations at existing restaurants, we also continued to expand our network. We opened 3 Haidilao restaurants and began putting resources in place for upcoming openings. We continue to explore additional brands and strengthen our shared support functions at headquarters. Related investment at this stage was higher than a year ago. Operating profit improved from the second quarter, but remained below the prior-year level. Let me walk you through our main initiatives this quarter. First, we stayed focused on restaurant operations and adapted guest engagement and staff management to each market.

    We continue to give regions and restaurants flexibility. Local teams could adjust how they operated based on local spending conditions, their guest mix and each restaurant's performance. We also stepped up frontline training, staffing and day-to-day management. As preparations for new openings progressed, we began recruiting and training for key roles in advance. To date, more than 60% of our restaurants have trained managers ready to step up. That gives us a talent pipeline for new openings and ongoing operations. In guest engagement, we put more weight on how much a campaign actually drives traffic and repeat visits alongside discounts it offers.

    Take Vietnam, our restaurants improved loyalty benefits, engaged staff to bring in fresh guests and maintained closer ties with guest communities. They also ran campaigns around local holidays and dining occasions. These efforts helped attract new guests and bring loyalty members back. Second, we continue to make Haidilao distinctive in each market. We stepped up local menu development and refined our menus, building on ingredients and dishes familiar to local guests. We tracked whether new dishes could sustain sales and generate repeat orders after launch. In Singapore, we introduced laksa hot pot and tender pork belly rolls, bringing familiar local flavors to hot pot.

    It has been revealed that in Korea, we focused on beef, specialty broths and snacks, launching thick-cut beef oyster blade, a rich chestnut and chicken broth and mini milk buns. In Vietnam, we introduced specialty beef and mushroom and vegetable platters to add more choices for local celebrations and group meals. Japan, Canada and Australia also kept adjusting their menus based on seasonal demand, ingredient quality and local taste. We track what guests order, which dishes they order again and how much revenue those dishes contribute. We use that data along with local supply conditions to adjust the menu mix. Our aim is to offer guests more choice while managing menus and running food operations more efficiently.

    It has been revealed that third, we continue to strengthen our shared support functions at headquarters. We built on our routine performance tracking by looking at more data together that included table turnover, operating data, member behavior, menu mix, marketing campaigns, costs and expenses. This helps regional teams pinpoint challenges and take actions. On the menu side, we use dish click-through rate, repeat orders, sales contribution and gross margin to guide menu changes and newly introduced item rolls out. In marketing, we review the returns on set menus and campaigns and assess their impact on traffic, sales and profit. Restaurants can then adjust pricing and promotions more swiftly. At the end of September, Haidilao had more than 10 million registered loyalty members overseas.

    Recent findings suggest that as the membership grows, we are focusing on keeping members active and turning that engagement into repeat spending. We look at how often different groups dine with us and how long they go between visits, so restaurants can tailor their outreach. We also share lessons across markets and translate our analysis into practical steps for restaurants. This helps headquarters provide more effective support to frontline teams. Fourth, we continue to expand the Haidilao network at a measured pace with close attention to how upcoming restaurants operate. We opened 3 Haidilao restaurants this quarter, bringing the overseas total to 132 at the end of September. One more has already opened in the fourth quarter and 6 others are preparing to open.

    Based on our current progress, we expect 13 openings for the full year. Local teams continue to identify opportunities based on market demand, changes in trade areas, the talent pipeline and projected investment returns. Headquarters supports them by visiting proposed sites, assessing management candidates, reviewing project risks and testing the assumptions behind projections. This helps us pace our openings. Fifth, we continue to advance the Pomegranate Strategy and test different restaurant formats across markets. At quarter end of this quarter, we operated 26 restaurants overseas under other brands. They included Malatang, Barbecue, Izakaya and Halal Hot Pot. Several concepts have begun to establish their operating models and show early signs of profitability.

    At Hi Bowl, our Malatang concept, we've developed a quick-service model with relatively high seat turnover and relatively low upfront investment. Our Canadian location has been profitable at the restaurant level for several consecutive months, and our Japanese location was profitable at the restaurant level throughout the quarter. Our Izakaya in Japan has also been profitable at the restaurant level for several consecutive months after we refined the menu mix and staffing. Performance still varies considerably across these concepts. The Pomegranate Plan as a whole is still in the investment and business model validation stage. For concepts that are performing well, we'll continue to refine the menu, supply chain and management model.

    Sources indicate that where results are below expectations, we'll keep making adjustments and carefully assess the next steps. Overall, we continued to improve existing restaurant operations this quarter while expanding our network and diversifying our business. As conditions evolve across markets, we'll keep our focus on both employees and guests. We'll strengthen the support headquarters provides, improve operations at each restaurant and keep the company on a steady path for long-term growth. Thank you. That concludes my review of third quarter operations. I'll now turn the call over to Lu Li to discuss our financial results.

    Lu Li: Thank you, Yu. Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining the call. I am Lu Li, the company's CFO. I'll walk you through Super Hi International's financial and operating results for the third quarter of 2026. Total revenue was $229 million, up 7.1% from $214 million a year ago and up 4.8% from the second quarter. Haidilao restaurant revenue was $206 million, up 2.4% year-over-year. We had a net increase of 6 Haidilao restaurants from a year ago. Overall table turnover and guest visits were also higher, which supported restaurant revenue. Beyond dine-in, we continue to invest in delivery and broaden the range of items available online. Delivery revenue was approximately $7.85 million, up approximately 77.3% year-over-year.

    Recent findings suggest that other revenue was approximately $15.9 million, up 78.7% year-over-year. It came mainly from sales of food products and seasonings from the Haidilao brand and our own central kitchens as well as restaurant revenue from new brands under the Pomegranate Plan. Turning to costs and expenses. Raw materials and consumables cost $79.611 million. Overall gross margin was 65.3%, down 1.4 percentage points year-over-year. Staff costs were $78.791 million or about 34.2% of revenue. That was up about 1 percentage point from 33.2% a year ago. Since the start of the year, we've continued to improve existing restaurant operations while steadily expanding Haidilao and our other brands. We began preparing new locations and putting staff in place ahead of openings.

    Preopening investment was higher than a year ago. We also strengthened the shared support functions at headquarters and stepped up investment in building and training our talent pipeline. At Haidilao restaurants, margins remained stable to slightly higher year-over-year. Part of the change in group-level costs reflects our continued investment in expansion and in strengthening those shared management capabilities. Rent and related expenses were $6.483 million or about 2.8% of revenue. Utilities were $8.284 million or about 3.6% of revenue. Both ratios were broadly flat year-over-year. Depreciation and amortization came to $22.384 million or about 9.8% of revenue, down 0.2 percentage points. Travel and other operating expenses were $28.987 million or about 10.9% of revenue, down about 0.2 percentage points.

    Those last 2 ratios fell mainly because revenue increased. Operating profit was approximately $9.933 million, with an operating margin of 4.3%. This mainly reflected the increased investment I mentioned in business expansion and management capabilities. Compared with the second quarter, operating profit rose by about 22.2% and operating margin increased by 0.6 percentage points from 3.7% to 4.3%. Profit after tax for this quarter was $9.226 million, up 155.6% from $3.593 million a year ago. We recorded a net foreign exchange gain of $4.63 million compared with a net foreign exchange loss of $5.813 million a year earlier. That was a positive swing of approximately $10.443 million.

    Sources indicate that this year-over-year increase in net profit was, therefore, driven mainly by the improvement in nonoperating foreign exchange results. Net cash generated from operating activities was $36.18 million, up 6.2% from $38.14 million a year ago. At September 30, 2026, bank balances and cash stood at approximately $243 million. Our liquidity remains strong. Let me now turn to our key restaurant metrics. At quarter end, we operated 132 Haidilao restaurants overseas. We recorded about 8.4 million guest visits this quarter, up about 3.7% year-over-year. Average table turnover was 4x per day, up 0.1 turn. Average spending per guest was $24.5, down approximately $0.1.

    That mainly reflected a shift in the guest mix with markets where guests spend less per visit accounting for a higher share of our traffic. Average daily revenue per restaurant was $17,700, down about 1.7% year-over-year. Same-store table turnover was 4x per day, up 0.1 turn. While turnover improved overall, changes in average spending per guest and traffic across regions continue to affect same-store sales. Group-wide same-store sales fell 2.3% year-over-year. Southeast Asia was broadly flat. East Asia grew, and same-store sales in North America and other regions remained under pressure. Let me now take a closer look at the figures by region. Performance varied considerably by region this quarter, with Southeast Asia and East Asia remaining broadly resilient.

    Sources indicate that we opened 2 Haidilao restaurants in Southeast Asia, 1 in Vietnam and 1 in Indonesia. Average table turnover rose from 3.7x to 4x per day year-over-year. Same-store turnover rose by 0.1 turn to 3.9x per day. Overall guest traffic improved. Average spending per guest was $18.7, down $0.4. At same stores, it was slightly higher at $19.2, down $0.1. The differences mainly reflect where the new restaurants opened. Higher table turnover helped lift average daily sales per restaurant by 0.6% to $15,600. Now in East Asia, average table turnover held at 4.9x per day. Same-store turnover was 5x per day, up 0.1 turn. Mature restaurants continue to perform well.

    Average spending per guest was $28.8, both overall and at same stores, down slightly year-over-year. This mainly reflected a weaker Japanese yen against the U.S. dollar. At constant exchange rates, overall spending per guest rose $0.40. Average daily sales per restaurant were $20,300, broadly flat year-over-year. We still see room for improvement in North America and other regions. As local dining habits and market conditions evolve, guests in some markets are paying closer attention to price and the dining experience. In some markets, the guest mix and what people want are also changing. That makes it more demanding for restaurants to attract new guests and retain existing ones. We opened 1 new Haidilao restaurant in the United States this quarter.

    In North America, both overall and same-store table turnover were 3.4x per day, down 0.6 and 0.5 turns respectively year-over-year. Average spending per guest was $41.5 overall and $40.8 at same stores, both were higher than a year ago. Since the start of the year, we've upgraded what's included in some of our North America set menus with slightly higher starting prices. Average daily sales per restaurant were $19,600, down about 11.3% year-over-year. Canada was the main drag on operating efficiency in the region. Our Canadian team continues to adjust pricing on individual dishes and set menus in line with local dining habits and price sensitivity. It is also offering set menus during off-peak hours to draw guests in.

    Sources indicate that in other regions, we operate 12 restaurants, all were open for more than 75 days in both the current and prior year quarters and are included in our same-store base. So the metrics are the same for both groups. Average table turnover was 3.5x per day, down 0.2 turn. Average spending per guest was $41.5, up $2.1 year-over-year. At constant exchange rates, it was up $0.20 or broadly flat. Lower turnover weighed on restaurant operating efficiency. Average daily sales per restaurant were $22,300, down about 2.6%. That concludes our review of the company's third quarter 2026 financial and operating results. Thank you. We'll now open the floor to questions from investors and analysts.

    Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question comes from Zheshang Securities. [ Ms. Zhong Yichen ], please go ahead.

    Sources indicate that unknown Analyst: My name is [ Zhong Yichen]. I actually have 2 questions. The first one is about overseas competition. More and more Chinese restaurant brands now are expanding overseas. The competition has intensified. How does competition vary by country? And what impact has it had on your table turnover and rents? How do you plan to respond as more brands go overseas? That's my first question. My second question is that, since the beginning of the year, Haidilao in China has been building shared support functions and gradually shifting some functional responsibilities away from restaurant managers. How far along are you overseas? Where do restaurant managers and regional teams still have discretion?

    Yu Li: Thank you, [ Ms. Zhong ], for your questions. Let me take both of your questions. Now regarding your first question, yes, indeed, more and more Chinese restaurant brands are right now entering the overseas market in recent years. That brings more competition, but it also helps familiarize consumers overseas with Chinese food and expands the market. In some Asia Pacific markets, demand for Chinese food is already well established and competition is more about how restaurants differentiate their menus and guest experience. In Europe and North America, there is still considerable room to build brands. We compete with Chinese restaurants and also a wide range of local operators as well.

    In a recent development, the impact on table turnover and rents varies by market. Turnover depends on consumer demands, traffic in the trade area and how well the restaurant is run, among other factors. Competition is one of those factors. When choosing new locations, we look at competition in the trade area, lease terms and also the return we need from the projects. We keep investment costs under tight control. We will keep focusing on both employees and guests. We'll develop more products for local tastes, improve our service experience and strengthen our loyalty program to reach more mainstream local diners. We believe lasting competitiveness comes down to the food, service and our ability to run individual restaurants well and consistently.

    It has been revealed that now regarding your second question, we are moving in the same direction as Haidilao in China. We want restaurant managers to spend more time on guests, staff and day-to-day operations. Shared tools and specialist support are gradually being centralized. Headquarters already provides shared support to regional teams in areas including digital systems, operating analysis, financial management and supply chain management. Dining habits, labor laws -- I mean, rules and supply conditions vary considerably from country to country. So we'll continue to give regional teams substantial operating autonomy and flexibility. Regions and restaurants can adapt product development, pricing, marketing, customer acquisition and staff management to local conditions. We maintain common standards for food safety, service quality and compliance.

    Shared support gives restaurant managers more time to focus on guests and employees while preserving frontline discretion and improving the quality and efficiency of restaurant operations. That's all for my answer.

    Operator: The next question comes from Shengwei Lai with CICC.

    Shengwei Lai: I am Shengwei Lai from CICC. I have 3 small questions. The first one is about North America. Well, what are your priorities for improving the North America business over the next few quarters? Which steps are most likely to make a meaningful difference in reaching mainstream local diners, driving repeat visits and improving your restaurant footprint? What do you expect to see? And when do you expect to see the results? My second question is about the restaurant growth outlook. Since the fourth quarter began, what changes have you seen in consumer demand and restaurant traffic in Southeast Asia, East Asia and North America? Looking ahead to next year, what will drive same-store growth by region?

    It has been revealed that and which markets are you most confident about? And my last question is about margin. Now we actually see that you have put in new investment this quarter. What will be the main levers for improving the group's operating margin next year? How much room is there to improve labor productivity, source locally and turn around underperforming restaurants? How will you pace investment in shared profit -- I mean, shared support functions as revenue grows?

    Yu Li: All right. This is Yu Li. I'm going to take your first question. Now regarding North America, North America has been affected by changes in demand and competition locally. We also have work to do on understanding the market, managing operations and responding more quickly. We were slow to spot and act on some market changes. We've begun restructuring the management team to strengthen local operations and help our teams pick up on changes sooner and execute faster. We're working on 3 fronts. First, we are reviewing and adjusting our local operating strategy to give guests more reasons to visit.

    Some restaurants have changed dishes and set menus based on market feedback, launched themed weekend events and focused more on students. We'll keep tracking what works and adjust our approach to each market and restaurant. Second, we are managing each restaurant more closely and refining the network. We'll take a closer look at traffic by location and time of the day, menu mix, staffing and operating costs. This will help us target improvements at individual restaurants. Third, we want to broaden our guest base. While retaining existing diners, we will reach out to more mainstream local guests with targeted products, campaigns and local marketing. We want to attract more new diners and gradually bring more of them back.

    Recent findings suggest that we hope to see early results from some marketing and operational changes over the next 1 to 2 quarters. It will take longer to assess shifts in the guest mix, where repeat visit rates settle and whether individual restaurants sustain their improvement. That's my answer for your first question. Now Ms. Lu Li is going to take the other 2 of your questions.

    Lu Li: Now regarding your second question, basically, overseas markets are moving into the traditional peak dining season. Demand for holiday and year-end group meals has increased. Traffic has improved overall, and table turnover is higher year-over-year. Some markets in East and Southeast Asia stood out, and East Asia as a whole held steady. Some North American restaurants remain under pressure. We're also seeing encouraging signs in demand for business gatherings and firm dinners. Our overseas restaurants are preparing to accommodate these groups and capture peak season demand. Looking ahead to 2027, we're confident that Southeast Asia and East Asia can maintain steady operations.

    Industry observers note that same-store growth will continue to come mainly from locally developed products, the loyalty program, repeat visits and closer management at the restaurant level. In North America, we'll focus on improving existing restaurants, reaching more mainstream local diners, refining our menu and pricing and getting more guests to act on our campaigns. Overall, our priority remains running each restaurant well. We'll make the most of the peak season and keep improving the guest experience and operating efficiency to support future same-store growth. Now regarding your last question, which is about our operating efficiency. There's room to improve profitability at existing restaurants. We make decisions with operating quality in mind and balance near-term performance with long-term development.

    At existing restaurants, we'll improve staffing and scheduling, strengthen procurement and source more locally. For restaurants that are falling short of expectations, we'll make targeted improvements or adjust the network. The aim is to improve efficiency and profitability at individual restaurants. Across the group, preparations for new Haidilao restaurants, new concepts under the Pomegranate Plan and shared support capabilities at headquarters all require upfront resources and investment that can affect group margins in the short term. We'll pace investment according to how the businesses evolve and what stage they're at and keep reviewing the returns on that spending. Overall, we're confident that we can keep improving profitability at existing restaurants.

    We will continue making the long-term investments we need and balance them with near-term operating performance to support steady, sustainable growth. Thank you.

With exchange rates still volatile, how do you quantify the point at which the trade-off between spending per guest and table turnover makes sense? Are you considering taking what has worked in Asia into new markets?

In East Asia, spending per guest rose by $0.40 at constant exchange rates. In North America, it rose by $2.6 year-over-year, mainly because we've refined, upgraded and introduced menu items since the first half of the year and adjusted some set menus.

    It has been revealed that in other regions, spending per guest rose by $0.20 at constant exchange rates, reflecting a small impact from menu changes. We believe that price sensitivity varies across markets, so pricing needs to vary too. In North America, the third quarter numbers show a clear impact on table turnover from changes in spending per guest. Market conditions and guest needs can change very promptly. We also realize that regional managers need to be closely involved in local operations so they can improve the experience while offering good value. When we weigh spending per guest against table turnover, we look at each restaurant's overall performance.

    Headquarters look at table turnover alongside the menu mix, returns on marketing spend and gross margins to help restaurants adjust pricing and promotions. So that was my answer for your first question. Regarding your second question, yes, we have operated in Southeast and East Asia for years and have built up considerable experience adapting to local markets. Third quarter average table turnover in Southeast Asia rose from 3.7x to 4x per day year-over-year. East Asia held at 4.9x. Overall operating metrics remain fairly resilient in both regions. What travels across markets is our expertise in site selection, talent development, supply chain management, menu development and restaurant operations.

    Recent findings suggest that but the menu mix, pricing and marketing still need to reflect local demand in each country. We'll look at both adding restaurants in existing markets and entering latest areas where we already have brand awareness, a supply chain and trained staff, and a denser network can improve operating efficiency. We'll also weigh coverage across trade areas, traffic at existing locations and whether a new restaurant could draw traffic away from them. For new regions and countries, we'll take a closer look at demand, spending power, competition, supply conditions and the availability of management talent. We've done some initial work in markets and some markets in Europe and South America, but it's still early, and there's a lot to do.

    In a recent development, site visits and deeper research will help us understand local conditions and prepare before we move ahead gradually. Our approach is still to identify opportunities from the ground up, with restaurant-level operating quality and long-term investment returns determining the pace of opening new stores. So that was my answer for your second question. The last question was about delivery. Now delivery has been one of our fastest-growing businesses over the past few quarters. In the third quarter of 2026, delivery revenue reached approximately $7.85 million, up 77.3% year-over-year and representing about 3.4% of group revenue. Delivery growth has come mainly from new products, marketing, broader distinction -- sorry, broader distribution and closer partnerships with local delivery platforms.

    Recent findings suggest that delivery serves different occasions and operates very differently from dine-in. The delivery menu mainly offers simple meals and single-person sets. On average, a meal for one costs less on delivery than when dining in, and gross margin is also slightly lower. Delivery has lower labor costs, but it also incurs extra costs such as platform commissions. That results in different cost and profit structures. Haidilao's core strengths are food, service and the in-restaurant experience. We'll protect the experience as we grow our delivery business. At each location, we consider kitchen capacity, staffing, how busy dine-in is and local delivery demand before deciding what to offer on which platform and how. Almost all Haidilao restaurants now offer delivery services.

    Sources indicate that we look at whether delivery generates incremental revenue and profit and makes a meaningful contribution. We don't set a fixed target for its share of revenue. That's all. Thank you.

Where concepts perform well, we will continue to build the capabilities they need. Where results fall short, we'll make timely adjustments. At the end of September, bank balances and cash were approximately $243 million. Overall, liquidity remains strong.

    In allocating capital, we will consider the funding needs of existing operations and planned investment in fresh Haidilao restaurants. As the program grows, we are refining the benefits at each membership tier.     Kanzhun (BZ +12.56%) management reported a period of transition in its monetization model and user expansion strategies. The tech giant implemented a pricing reform in Tier 1 cities, replacing free job listings with a paid structure to improve listing quality and user satisfaction. Management stated that blue-collar workers and small-to-medium enterprises in lower-tier cities remain primary growth drivers, while manufacturing demand showed resilience compared to other lagging sectors like automobile and retail. At the same time, some ultralow-priced job listings costing as little as RMB 1 per job per day has created the escape phenomenon mentioned above. Throughout, we took a deliberately measured approach, rolling the experiment out gradually, testing and learning as we went, which is why it takes time, and even at prices after the completed reforms in those Tier 1 cities based on our research, there is still reasonable potential for us to be continuously tapped. Those potential could be expanded further. As long as the recruiters continue to do the recruitment on the platform, their goal is to harvest job seekers faster and more accurately.

Then, the average price of a job posting, which is around RMB 4 to RMB 6 per day, is actually a very low price. Since the price reform experiment, so far, the recruiter acceptance has been good. The revenue has increased and job seeker satisfaction has improved markedly, especially in those experimented areas. The constraints caused by the recruiter escape have decreased significantly as well.     The Future Is Brighter Than You Think: Why Technology Could Make Humanity Better Off

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lindsey Witmer Collins is Founder and CEO of WLCM.AI, an Inc.
    • Recent findings suggest that ​I know how that sounds, and I know it makes me seem uninformed or naive, but I’m really just trying to make an important choice thoughtfully.
    • Our feeds show many flavors of doom: AI is coming for the jobs, the planet is cooking, the kids can’t look up from their phones and somewhere a robot is learning to do backflips.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lindsey Witmer Collins is Founder and CEO of WLCM.AI, an Inc. 5000 company building AI solutions for enterprises, and Scribbly Books.

    Recent findings suggest that ​I know how that sounds, and I know it makes me seem uninformed or naive, but I’m really just trying to make an important choice thoughtfully. It’s a choice we all get to make: How do I orient myself to the world I’m in and the one I’m building? And, specifically, I’m curious. What if we ran our projections for the future of humanity in the opposite direction than the doom default? In other words, what if the future is awesome?

    Our feeds show many flavors of doom: AI is coming for the jobs, the planet is cooking, the kids can’t look up from their phones and somewhere a robot is learning to do backflips. I build software for a living, including the kind people are nervous about, so I’m not saying this from a hammock. I’m looking for evidence.

    A good place to understand where we’re going is to see where we’ve been—to understand what we care about, what we’re capable of and what direction, as a species, we trend toward.

    If you were born in 1800, there was, globally, roughly a 43% chance you’d die before your fifth birthday. Today, it’s about 4%, and in most of the world it’s lower than that. Nearly 80% of humanity lived in extreme poverty two centuries ago; by 2019 it was under 10%, and since 1990 the count has dropped by something like 130,000 people every single day. In 1820, 1 adult in 10 could read. We’re at 87% now.

    Industry observers note that none of that happened by accident. It happened because somebody figured out that germs exist, that a cowpox sore could stop smallpox, that nitrogen could be pulled out of thin air and turned into fertilizer. Somebody built the sewer. Somebody built the washing machine—Hans Rosling used to call it the greatest invention of the industrial revolution, and his argument was basically that it gave his mother back enough hours to read to him.

    My great-grandmother could walk into my kitchen today—hot water out of a wall, a box that keeps food cold, a cabinet of medicine that works, the whole of recorded human knowledge in the pocket of my jeans—and conclude she had died and gone to heaven. To me it’s just Monday, and I’m a little annoyed about the traffic.

    Sources indicate that the pace never slowed down; the headlines just moved on to other things. The International Energy Agency called solar the cheapest electricity in history back in 2020, and it has kept getting cheaper. Lithium-ion battery packs ended 2025 averaging $108 per kilowatt-hour, down 93% since 2010, which is the reason the grid, my electric car and the battery in my lawnmower are all getting electrified without a modicum of drama.

    In December 2023, the FDA approved the first CRISPR-based therapy, for people with sickle cell disease—a disease we’ve understood at the molecular level for decades and could do very little about until now. Twenty-five African countries now give malaria vaccines as part of routine childhood shots, and they’re more than 39 million doses in. This year, four astronauts flew around the moon for the first time since 1972, and an mRNA flu shot got approved after beating the traditional one by about 27% in a trial of nearly 50,000 people.

    According to recent reports, and AI—which we love to fret about—is mostly busy doing the routable work: the reading, the sorting, the first draft, the thousand small lookups. That raises the value of everything it can’t reach, and most of what it can’t reach is other people.

    I spend most of my time now on an above-ground mining startup focused on the critical minerals and materials sitting in the U.S.’s retiring infrastructure—EV batteries, solar panels, telecom copper wires and so forth. A surprising share of the next decade’s supply is already here, waiting to be recovered, and it’s on the verge of happening.

    What if we get all of the benefits of technology, and we still love each other, and hang out, and chat with the person at the checkout?

    Picture a backyard cookout in 2075. Grandma is 120 and bringing her famous potato salad, because the cataract fix was an afternoon, her hip came out of a printer and she’s been weightlifting her entire adult life. The power for the whole event—the grill, the speaker, the car that drove her over—cost roughly nothing, because sunlight is free and we finally got good at storing it. The toddler running laps around the table will learn of malaria only in history books. Somebody’s cousin runs a three-person manufacturer that would have needed 40 people in 2020. And we’re still watching live sports in the living room.

    If the lines on the charts to keep going the way they’ve gone for 200 years, and if we keep showing up with a side dish, we might end up better than fine.

    Sources indicate that we’re all makers and builders in our own unique ways, and we build what we see in our mind’s eye. If the only future we picture is the grim one, we might start driving off the road.

    I’m going to say we’re building a beautiful and abundant future, and that things will keep getting better. You may say I’m choosing my facts selectively, and you would be correct. There are too many facts, so we all get our pick.

    Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

    #108168. Ready for ‘The Great Lock In’? Viral Money Trend Can Improve Focus

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (809 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nerdwallet ↗ Open Full Page

    Ready for ‘The Great Lock In’? Viral Money Trend Can Improve Focus

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some new money goals and make progress toward them.
    • That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.
    • “You’re probably not doing too much,” notes Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some new money goals and make progress toward them.

    That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.

    “You’re probably not doing too much,” notes Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan. “It gets dark early. So those can be great months to lock into saving and not spend in excess.”.

    One vital component of the Great Lock In is developing upcoming routines that will last well into 2027, claims Jordan Mangaliman, founder and fiduciary wealth advisor at GoldLine Wealth Management in Fullerton, California.

    “We want a long-term habit versus a Band-Aid fix,” he says. “In today’s economy, money goes in and out so blindingly fast.”.

    Industry observers note that ready to join the movement? Here’s how to get started.

    What’s your money moonshot? Maybe it’s paying off all your credit card debt or purchasing a home. Or spending less than you earn. Defining it is the first step toward achieving it.

    It has been revealed that “Spend a lot of time identifying what that goal is,” Baird indicates. “Everyone’s in a different position, so comparing yourself to what you see online might not be applicable.”.

    Even while setting ambitious money goals, it’s worth grounding them in reality, Mangaliman indicates.

    If you want to save a larger portion of your income, he suggests trying the fresh saving pattern for a couple of months to see how it feels rather than saying you’ll do it forever and then getting frustrated.

    “It’s a marathon, not a sprint,” Mangaliman adds.

    Once you’ve outlined those major goals for your Great Lock In, create a budget to help you achieve them, Baird states.

    Industry observers note that he suggests combing through your previous credit or debit card spending to see where your money is going. Then you can decide what you want to change or shift. Using a tool like the 50/30/20 budget calculator can also help. This approach allots 50% of take-home pay toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings and debt payments beyond the minimum.

    According to recent reports, baird suggests including saving as a line item in your budget so you don’t forget to do it. “Building that cost into your budget will put you in a better position later,” he states.

    Any Great Lock In should include growing your savings, because that makes achieving other goals easier, Baird states.

    Recent findings suggest that “Maybe there’s something you could cut in the short term to build up that savings,” he notes. Good targets include subscription services, food delivery, entertainment and travel costs.

    Saving more is especially challenging in today’s environment, when everyday expenses like gas are higher than they were a year ago.

    It has been revealed that baird states that makes winter a good time to try to reduce costs. There can be fewer temptations to go out and spend money when the days are shorter and the temperatures are colder.

    Mangaliman recommends setting aside three to six months’ worth of expenses, although even a smaller amount is helpful. “Ultimately it’s about what you can afford,” he says. “It’s the foundation of your financial house.”.

    Along with building savings, paying down high-interest debt is another pillar of the Great Lock In.

    Industry observers note that with credit card interest rates higher than they were a few years ago, carrying credit card debt has gotten more expensive. “I would consider applying some savings to paying down debt, especially right now when your debt is costing you more than you can earn in savings,” Baird notes. (You still want to reserve an emergency fund to cover unexpected expenses.).

    According to recent reports, “High-interest debt is one of the biggest thieves of wealth,” Mangaliman states. And one way to avoid turning to debt again in the future is to build up that emergency fund so it’s there for you if you need it.

    According to recent reports, even when you are committed to a Great Lock In, some hiccups along the way are inevitable. Success depends on continuing anyway.

    According to recent reports, “It’s like a diet,” Baird says. “Just because you ate ice cream on a Sunday doesn’t mean on Monday you can’t go right back to being disciplined again.”.

    “Be kind to yourself and do everything in moderation,” Mangaliman suggests. Just wanting to improve your finances is already a great first step, he indicates.

    In fact, he embraces the Great Lock In mentality himself. “There’s an old saying: It’s not how you start, but how you finish,” he says. “And you want to finish the year on a strong note so you carry those habits into 2027 and beyond.”.

    #108166. The AI Infrastructure Bet That Smart Enterprises Are Making

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (904 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    The AI Infrastructure Bet That Smart Enterprises Are Making

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Paul Deraval, Cofounder & CEO of NinjaCat, is a software veteran with 20+ years driving innovation in martech, AI and agency growth.
    • Right now, companies of all sizes and sectors are racing to adopt artificial intelligence.
    • Industry observers note that for many enterprises, this means increasing access to AI tools.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Paul Deraval, Cofounder & CEO of NinjaCat, is a software veteran with 20+ years driving innovation in martech, AI and agency growth.

    Right now, companies of all sizes and sectors are racing to adopt artificial intelligence. Many consider AI the next big thing, and no one wants to miss out.

    Industry observers note that for many enterprises, this means increasing access to AI tools. They are paying for Claude subscriptions, licensing ChatGPT Enterprise and rolling out Microsoft Copilot across departments. According to Gallup’s latest workplace survey, 47% of employees say their organization integrated AI tools in Q2 2026, up from 41% the previous quarter.

    Unfortunately, more tools don’t necessarily equate to better outcomes or higher productivity, and many executives aren’t seeing ROI even as they spend millions on software seats and infrastructure. A National Bureau of Economic Research study found that 89% of executives reported AI had “no impact on labor productivity.” ​.

    In a recent development, companies have real reasons to be excited about AI, but those that use it to gain a competitive advantage and add real value will invest in the governance and infrastructure needed to operationalize these models effectively at scale. As Forbes contributor Güney Yıldız reports: “AI spend does not become ROI simply because usage goes up. Value capture requires workflow redesign, not just license distribution.”​.

    Here’s how forward-thinking leaders can redesign workflows to achieve real ROI from their AI investments.

    AI should deliver tangible outcomes like making work easier, better or cheaper. Its purpose is not, as many leaders mistakenly assume, to simply increase AI adoption or add another tool to the technology stack.​.

    Recent findings suggest that executives can be forgiven for misunderstanding that point. Adoption can feel like action, and they face immense pressure to act. In reality, enterprises have different teams, roles and workflows, each with its own needs. Some can benefit from an AI tool or autonomous agent while others really don’t.

    Rather than forcing an AI tool or agentic layer into every process, match AI capabilities to a specific problem. Right now, many businesses conflate success with usage. However, as the tokenmaxxing debacle shows, measuring usage isn’t the same as promoting real impact.

    It has been revealed that instead of just measuring AI use, audit workflow bottlenecks before selecting tools so their capabilities match the problem they’re trying to solve. At the same time, prioritize tools that embed directly into existing systems, so workflows stay integrated and frictionless. If a tool can’t integrate directly with CRM, ERP or other core systems of record, its organizational impact will be limited.

    The enterprise technology stack is already crowded with companies deploying hundreds of apps and SaaS solutions. Many work independently, disconnected from the disparate app ecosystem surrounding companies big and small. Adding upcoming AI tools to this mix has limited impact and can even create more work for employees. Effective AI adoption that justifies AI spend will go beyond tools that answer questions or generate generic content. It will involve AI solutions that can proactively identify opportunities, recommend actions and even execute work. ​.

    For example, in marketing, where AI ad spending alone will top $32 billion in 2026, effective AI adoption could mean onboarding a solution that detects campaign performance problems, identifies underappreciated opportunities across a campaign or helps implement improvements to existing campaign collateral.

    Industry observers note that to maximize AI’s impact, invest in tools that make this possible and clarify the human element. Clearly define when AI can act independently, when approval is required and when humans must take the lead. ​.

    Combining the right tools with the right purpose in structured workflows, with clear roles and responsibilities, is the best way to invest in AI that gets work done.

    Sources indicate that AI is only as useful as the information and context it can access. Without clean, unified and reliable data, outputs can be inaccurate, inconsistent or disconnected from business priorities. Before making significant AI investments, smart enterprises will focus on organizing the technology they already have, connecting systems and simplifying workflows so AI can operate within business realities.​.

    Focus on infrastructure that connects AI to relevant business data, organizational knowledge and workflows while respecting role-based permissions and account-level boundaries.​.

    Sources indicate that understandably, security is foundational to these efforts. It can’t be bolted on later or retroactively applied. A governed environment, or “sandbox,” is a good place to start. Here, businesses can define what AI can access, what actions it can take and when it needs human approval.​.

    Sources indicate that boosting productivity is great, but it shouldn’t come at the expense of data security or privacy. Clear accountability, auditability and oversight help businesses scale AI without losing control over sensitive data or consequential decisions.​.

    Customers aren’t inherently impressed by a organization’s AI strategy, and neither are boards or shareholders. Everyone is looking for results.

    That’s why the competitive advantage comes from how well organizations connect AI to their data, people, processes and business goals. It’s the product of organizations that build the right foundation, enabling AI to do the right work with the right context and under the right controls.

    Investing in these fundamentals may not make headlines, but it’s the AI infrastructure bet that smart enterprises are making to deliver lasting business value.​.

    #108159. 4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (751 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nerdwallet ↗ Open Full Page

    4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.
    • Recent findings suggest that have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year?
    • If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

    Recent findings suggest that have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

    But what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

    Dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he remarked in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”.

    Don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:.

    Last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, notes Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

    If systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, mentioned Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good plan, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?).

    Recent findings suggest that “My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson mentioned. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”.

    If your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

    “This is the step I push hardest,” Judge states. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”.

    According to recent reports, if you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” notes Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”.

    It has been revealed that make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

    According to recent reports, keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

    Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

    Recent findings suggest that take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

    It has been revealed that and set a reminder to update your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the substantial concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he notes. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

    It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

    “The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” noted Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”.

    10 stocks we like better than NuScale Power ›.

    NuScale Power (SMR -1.51%) can still brag that it has the only small modular reactor (SMR) design approved by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Still, it's not as if this achievement has given way to NuScale entering the commercialization stage.

    In fact, as it stands now, the early-stage nuclear technology organization is earning more from interest on bank deposits than from reactors. This needs to change, fast. Otherwise, the stock, already down nearly 82% over the past year, could plunge further.

    Take a look at NuScale's latest quarterly results, and one could make the argument, albeit a stretch, that this stock is basically a certificate of deposit (CD) that happens to own an unprofitable nuclear start-up. That is, last quarter, the company generated just $281,000 in revenue from its operating business. Meanwhile, the company reported $19.1 million in investment income, aka income generated from its $933 million in reported cash and short-term investments.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Sources indicate that this interest income is hardly a silver bullet for NuScale. While it may have generated nearly 68 times as much from its cash as it did from its operating activities, the $19.1 million only partially covered NuScale's $64.8 million in operating losses during the quarter. Worse yet, as cash burn depletes its war chest, barring another capital raise, investment income will undoubtedly decline in the coming quarters.

    Sources indicate that the exclusive commercialization partnership with ENTRA1 Energy is a major hurdle for NuScale. ENTRA1 may have entered a collaboration agreement with the Tennessee Valley Authority to supply it with SMR-generated nuclear power, but the agreement is not yet binding. Add in other hurdles, and it may not be until the 2030s that this deal yields significant revenue for NuScale Power.

    Barring faster-than-expected progress with this catalyst, or the emergence of new commercial partnerships, consider it best to stay away from this stock. It may differ from other nuclear energy stocks, but with NuScale, the risk/reward proposition remains unfavorable.

    #108156. How Legacy Data Pipelines Become A Liability When AI Moves From Chat To Action

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1035 w)

    How Legacy Data Pipelines Become A Liability When AI Moves From Chat To Action

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that prashanthi Kolluru is the founder of KloudPortal.
    • In enterprise data engineering initiatives, I’ve noticed an often-overlooked pattern: a data pipeline can be judged successful simply because it runs as expected.
    • According to recent reports, this is becoming increasingly significant as enterprises move from AI assistants that retrieve information to agents that execute tasks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that prashanthi Kolluru is the founder of KloudPortal. Helping global capability centers (GCCs) hire product-ready engineering pods.

    In enterprise data engineering initiatives, I’ve noticed an often-overlooked pattern: a data pipeline can be judged successful simply because it runs as expected. Data moves between systems, scheduled jobs complete, reports are delivered and the business keeps operating smoothly. Yet the same pipeline may rely on assumptions about data freshness, transformation logic, quality and business rules that become challenging to manage as requirements evolve.​.

    According to recent reports, this is becoming increasingly significant as enterprises move from AI assistants that retrieve information to agents that execute tasks. An AI agent operating within an enterprise workflow may use incorrect information to revision records, initiate processes or influence business decisions without anyone realizing it.​.

    This shift has prompted me to examine more closely the weaknesses that may have been manageable in traditional analytics environments but become more critical when AI is integrated into operational workflows.

    Five areas deserve particular attention before organizations extend AI agents into consequential workflows.

    According to recent reports, A pipeline that refreshes data overnight may be perfectly adequate for a historical sales report. It can be unsuitable for an agent making decisions that depend on current inventory, account balances or order status.

    Industry observers note that the risk depends on the business decision, not simply on how old the data is. A delay of several hours may have little impact on one workflow and materially change the outcome of another.

    Technology leaders should define acceptable data freshness for each AI use case. Some workflows may need event-driven updates; others may work with scheduled processing. Rebuilding every pipeline for real-time delivery is rarely necessary. The goal is to match data availability to the consequences of acting on it.

    Legacy pipelines often rely on scripts and mappings that embed source-specific assumptions and business rules. When engineers introduce a upcoming system or data source, they may need to modify multiple parts of the pipeline and retest downstream dependencies.

    This becomes harder as AI agents need information from more enterprise systems and business context changes more frequently.

    It has been revealed that metadata-driven pipeline architecture offers one way to reduce this maintenance burden. Source mappings, transformation rules, validation checks and load configurations can be managed as metadata that a reusable framework interprets. This can make changes easier to manage than repeatedly modifying hard-coded procedures.

    Metadata alone, however, does not guarantee flexibility. Business rules still need clear ownership, version control and testing. Otherwise, an organization simply moves its complexity from code into configuration.

    Sources indicate that A missing field or duplicate record in a dashboard may be noticed during a review. The same defect, consumed by an AI agent, could influence a subsequent workflow before a person examines the underlying data.

    Industry observers note that consider customer records that use inconsistent identifiers across systems. An agent combining those records could associate an instruction with the wrong account if the pipeline fails to resolve the inconsistency.

    Validation therefore needs to go beyond checking whether a pipeline completed successfully. Teams should test completeness, uniqueness, relationships between records, acceptable ranges and relevant business rules. Where checks fail, the system should flag or quarantine affected data rather than silently passing it downstream.

    The appropriate controls depend on the use case, but the principle is consistent: successful data movement is not proof of trustworthy data.

    When an AI-assisted workflow produces an unexpected result, teams need to establish which source records were used, how those records were transformed and which business definitions applied at the time.

    That investigation becomes difficult when dependencies are undocumented, transformations are scattered across scripts or data definitions differ between systems. Without reliable lineage, teams may struggle to reproduce an outcome or identify where an error entered the pipeline.

    Organizations should maintain traceable data flows, versioned transformations and monitoring that connects pipeline failures to downstream use cases. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework can also help teams structure their approach to identifying, assessing and managing AI-related risks.

    For workflows with significant business consequences, treat the ability to reconstruct the data path as an operational requirement, not merely a documentation exercise. ​.

    A pipeline may deliver accurate account information to an agent, but access to that information should not automatically authorize the agent to initiate a payment, change a customer record or approve a transaction.

    These are separate decisions: what data a system can read, what actions it can perform and which actions require human approval.

    As organizations connect agents to enterprise applications, they should define permissions around specific operations, use appropriate controls for higher-risk actions and retain audit trails of what the agent accessed and did. Access policies should apply to the agent’s identity and the workflow it operates within, not simply to the data source.

    It has been revealed that data engineering and AI governance need to work together here. A well-governed pipeline cannot compensate for unrestricted action permissions, just as a tightly controlled agent cannot make unreliable data trustworthy. ​.

    It has been revealed that modernizing a legacy data environment does not necessarily mean replacing every pipeline or moving every workload to real-time processing. It starts with understanding which data feeds support AI workflows and what can happen when those feeds are delayed, incomplete or incorrect.

    Industry observers note that can technology leaders assess those pipelines against five practical questions: Is the data fresh enough for the decision? Are transformations understandable and maintainable? Are quality failures detected before the data is used? Can you reconstruct the source and transformation history? Are data permissions and agent action permissions clearly separated?

    Enterprises should avoid treating AI readiness as a separate layer added on top of existing data infrastructure. Pipeline design, maintenance and governance will influence what AI agents can safely do with enterprise information.

    In a recent development, organizations should examine these foundations early in AI planning rather than discover their limitations after agents become embedded in critical workflows. Modernization should reflect the business consequences of each use case and give AI agents a dependable basis for action.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

    Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

    It has been revealed that robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

    Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

    Recent findings suggest that robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the manufacturer has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

    Recent findings suggest that transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

    Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

    Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

    Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

    —With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney.

    #108151. Cross-Functional Collaboration Is Fashion’s Latest Competitive Advantage

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (856 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Cross-Functional Collaboration Is Fashion’s Latest Competitive Advantage

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Maximilien Abadie, Deputy CEO and a member of the Executive Committee, Lectra.
    • ​Speed and creativity have always been defining features of the fashion industry.
    • Companies that create the digital and cultural infrastructure to support cross-functional collaboration make it possible to unify workflows, anticipate challenges earlier and share data for faster, better decisions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Maximilien Abadie, Deputy CEO and a member of the Executive Committee, Lectra.

    ​Speed and creativity have always been defining features of the fashion industry. In a climate marked by fragmentation and continuing volatility, accelerating time to market and achieving the all-key five R’s (right place, right product, right price, right quantities and right consumer) have become less about moving faster at individual stages and more about improving how information is shared and decisions are made across the value chain.

    Companies that create the digital and cultural infrastructure to support cross-functional collaboration make it possible to unify workflows, anticipate challenges earlier and share data for faster, better decisions. This transforms the way a firm creates, manufactures and sells their products. ​.

    It has been revealed that every product that makes it to market is shaped by contributions from hundreds of different individuals, many of whom do not speak the same language or share a common perspective. The linear, step-by-step approach to collection development—design followed by development, then production and ending with marketing, merchandising and e-commerce—struggles to provide the agility needed to respond swiftly to the dynamism that characterizes this industry.

    When design, production and sales teams work as separate entities, each with their own tools, data and objectives, decision-making is slower and inefficiencies are greater. A feasibility problem discovered in production could have been identified at the development stage. Consumer insights gathered during the marketing phase are not passed on to creative teams. These disconnects can result in missed sales opportunities, excess inventory and frustrated customers. ​.

    According to recent reports, cross-functional collaboration supported by shared data contributes to greater resilience, innovation and growth. Research shows that cross-functional, team-focused transformations can drive a 30% increase in efficiency. When information flows freely across an interconnected value chain, decisions happen faster, errors are identified earlier and fewer resources are wasted.

    One of the most tangible benefits of data-based collaboration is its impact on time to market, which remains a critical challenge for global fashion brands. While some fashion players can develop and launch products in a matter of days, others still operate on timelines of six to nine months. Closing this gap requires rethinking product development from the earliest creative stages and ensuring continuity of information across the entire product life cycle.

    Beyond improving collaboration, these solutions help preserve and scale expertise by making institutional knowledge, technical know-how and historical product data accessible across the organization. Along with accelerating onboarding and decision-making, this helps brands ensure that valuable expertise is retained and leveraged across generations of teams.

    It has been revealed that data-based collaboration requires a shared infrastructure capable of integrating multiple functions and partners. Solutions embedded with AI and digitalization are the key enablers of this transformation. While product life cycle management (PLM) solutions remain essential for product data management, governance and life cycle visibility, a new generation of AI-enabled product development solutions is emerging to support the day-to-day workflow of bringing a product from concept to production.

    By bringing together internal teams, as well as a brand’s global network of suppliers, subcontractors and partners, these solutions ensure that all stakeholders are aligned and working from the same up-to-date information. Companies can capture and communicate data on designs, tech packs, materials, costs, timelines and suppliers in a common framework that cross-functional teams can rely on as products progress.

    When each team member has a 360-degree vision of the product in its journey, there are fewer surprises and improved coordination.

    The case for shared data infrastructure becomes even more urgent in light of upcoming traceability and sustainability regulations. The Digital Product Passport (DPP), part of the European Union’s Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, will require products sold in the EU in 2027 to carry structured, standardized product information. Even in the early phase of implementation, which will be a minimal, simplified version of the digital product passport, companies will be expected to provide data on material composition, origin, carbon footprint, supply chain traceability, recyclability, care, durability and chemical compliance.

    Recent findings suggest that compliance will require alignment across the full product cycle. While the first phase will most likely only require supply chain traceability up to Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers, adopting a digital traceability approach that starts with the original fibers that will eventually be used in garments and other products provides the foundation for visibility across all tiers of the supply chain. Artificial intelligence is a key enabler of this tracing technology. It continuously monitors transactions to detect inconsistencies or fraudulent claims, enabling brands to move from theoretical commitments to proven actions. Companies that build this infrastructure now will be positioned to leverage transparency as a competitive advantage.

    Collaborative solutions are reshaping how work is organized, executed and experienced. Beyond enabling basic communication, they support fresh ways of working that emphasize shared visibility and consistency across teams. In a business environment increasingly characterized by volatility, complexity and rapid change, these platforms are becoming an notable enabler for companies seeking to operate more efficiently and quickly.
