    #108149. When Days Matter: Navigating The AI-Accelerated Exploit Lifecycle

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1055 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    When Days Matter: Navigating The AI-Accelerated Exploit Lifecycle

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Eoin Keary Founder & CEO of Edgescan, an enterprise CTEM (Continuous Testing and Exposure Management platform) used by Fortune 500s.
    • In a recent development, ​AI is fundamentally changing the velocity of the threat landscape, particularly the time between vulnerability discovery and weaponization.
    • This creates a fresh imperative: Security processes designed around periodic assessment and remediation must evolve to operate at the speed of continuous change.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Eoin Keary Founder & CEO of Edgescan, an enterprise CTEM (Continuous Testing and Exposure Management platform) used by Fortune 500s.

    In a recent development, ​AI is fundamentally changing the velocity of the threat landscape, particularly the time between vulnerability discovery and weaponization. Vulnerabilities that historically took months, or even up to a year, to become active exploits can now move into the wild within days. AI also expands the attack surface itself as organizations deploy AI systems and agents across their environments, including systems that may not be fully visible to security teams.​.

    This creates a fresh imperative: Security processes designed around periodic assessment and remediation must evolve to operate at the speed of continuous change. They should consider a different approach to security that employs AI to manage data volume while retaining a human in the loop for critical decision making. In this way, their organizations can rise with the tide of AI-driven threats by purifying their cybersecurity data to ensure it remains manageable and actionable.​.

    The fundamental challenge in vulnerability management has never been finding vulnerabilities but determining which findings represent genuine, actionable risk. Organizations must distinguish between false positives, vulnerabilities that are real but not exploitable and vulnerabilities that are exploitable but mitigated by other controls.​.

    Only after those layers of validation can security teams determine which remaining vulnerabilities represent the greatest business risk and should be addressed first. AI threatens to amplify the existing “vulnerability noise” problem by dramatically increasing the volume of findings entering the security team’s workflow. The answer can’t be asking already-constrained security and development teams to manually process an increasingly powerful “firehose” of alerts.​.

    According to recent reports, slowing down detection isn’t the answer. A better answer is to add a validation layer between detection and action. The value of continuous assessment is its ability to provide a more current view of the environment. Without validation, however, it just produces more noise, faster. This is especially notable as AI accelerates both vulnerability discovery and vulnerability exploitation.

    The temptation to use AI to automate remediation and allow systems to patch vulnerabilities without human intervention is obvious.​ Yet autonomous remediation can introduce significant operational risk when an AI system lacks the business context necessary to understand the consequences of its actions. AI should be used to make security professionals “more bionic,” processing information, accelerating analysis and supporting decisions, while humans retain responsibility for critical remediation decisions.​.

    As for technical vulnerability data, it alone is insufficient to determine what an organization should fix first. Effective prioritization requires context about the affected asset, its criticality, its role in the business, its data flows and the potential consequences of exploitation. AI can help organizations apply and process this context at scale, but only if the underlying security data is accurate, validated and meaningful.

    In a recent development, for teams already buried in findings, the promise of less noise is appealing. The questions start when we discuss what adopting it involves. How much of their time will we need? Will it work with their existing tools? Will the findings arriving on their desks actually be any better?

    According to recent reports, in conversations with customers and prospective clients, these are always understandable concerns. They’ve heard plenty of promises about making security simpler. They want to know how much work it’ll take to get started and how much work it’ll save them afterwards. Sending over a mountain of alerts and wishing the team good luck is a fairly generous interpretation of helping.

    Recent findings suggest that providers need to be clear about who does the work. If we offer validated findings, the validation is our responsibility. It’s important to establish which findings are real and investigate exploitability and assess relevant controls before passing the results to the customer.

    Industry observers note that trust is another hurdle. Fewer findings can sound suspicious when the industry has spent years presenting bigger numbers as evidence of a better job. Customers need to see why something has been ruled out or deprioritized, what testing supports that decision and what remains uncertain.

    Industry observers note that “AI stated so” isn’t an explanation I’d fancy taking into a board meeting. Show the evidence and let people challenge the conclusion.​.

    Privacy and operational security deserve direct answers. What data will the provider access, and where will it be processed? What testing is permitted, and who approved it? Clear boundaries, documented data handling and named responsibilities help customers assess this service properly. They shouldn’t need a detective to work out what they’re signing up for.

    Yes, cost always comes up, but the subscription is only part of the calculation. Investigating false positives, chasing findings that can’t be reproduced and passing inconclusive tickets between teams all costs money. Those hours don’t become free because they’re missing from the procurement spreadsheet. Providers must demonstrate the reduction in effort for the client and explain the price they charge.

    The practical route is to start with a defined scope and agree what success looks like with security development and the budget owner. Measure the time spent investigating findings, the quality of evidence reaching developers and how quickly confirmed risks receive attention. Make implementation manageable, work with existing systems and show the results. That gives each team a reason to support adoption.​​.

    Industry observers note that organizations need greater visibility into their attack surface and a continuous understanding of what they’re trying to secure. Continuous assessment and visibility will become increasingly important as the pace of vulnerability discovery and exploitation accelerates. However, continuous assessment inevitably creates more data, making validation and suppression of irrelevant or low-value findings increasingly important.

    Industry observers note that organizations should prioritize security approaches that continuously assess the environment while filtering, validating and contextualizing findings before they reach security and development teams. The ultimate objective isn’t to automate every security decision but to ensure that even as the volume of cybersecurity data grows exponentially, organizations can reduce that information to a manageable number of accurate, contextual and actionable risks.​.

    In an AI-accelerated threat landscape, the organizations best positioned to respond will be those that can rise with the tide by purifying their cybersecurity data rather than drowning in it.​​.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There has been a ton of news in the stock market recently.
    • While looking at Security and Exchange Commission (SEC) documents may sound a tad boring, these documents reveal what trades billionaire hedge fund managers made in the third quarter.
    • In a recent development, one billionaire that I follow is David Tepper and his fund, Appaloosa Management.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Keithen Drury – Nov 25, 2026 at 2:00PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Micron Technology ›.

    There has been a ton of news in the stock market recently. Nvidia is making headlines with its CEO controversy and third-quarter earnings. Newly public Anthropic went public with a lot of fanfare. However, there was another event that occurred this week that flew under the radar of most investors: 13-F releases.

    While looking at Security and Exchange Commission (SEC) documents may sound a tad boring, these documents reveal what trades billionaire hedge fund managers made in the third quarter. Those are valuable pieces of information, as they show what the smart money is doing.

    In a recent development, one billionaire that I follow is David Tepper and his fund, Appaloosa Management. Tepper made some interesting moves during Q3. The most noteworthy was loading up on Micron Technology (MU -4.53%) shares while completely exiting his Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -1.75%) position.

    That's quite the call, but is it the right one?

    According to recent reports, david Tepper. Image source: Getty Images.

    Industry observers note that information available from 13-Fs naturally lags the market. The SEC requires funds with over $100 million in investments to disclose their end-of-quarter holdings and make those public 45 days after the quarter ends. This gives some buffer between filing and release date, which protects the fund's investments.

    However, investors need to be careful not to follow these documents too closely, as the landscape may have shifted from the end of the quarter to now.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Sources indicate that AMD is in that boat, because it has lost about 20% of its value since Q3 ended. That justifies Tepper's move and makes it appear that his fund took gains before a sell-off occurred. The reason? Likely AMD's valuation.

    AMD's stock has had a great year this year, but not all of that success has come from business growth. Instead, the market has chosen to give AMD a far higher premium this year than it has in the past. Reaching about 35 times next year's earnings at the end of Q3, it signaled that it was time to sell the stock.

    AMD PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts.

    Tepper did exactly that, and I think that was a smart move, because there was just too much hype baked into AMD's stock price. Buying Micron was an interesting pivot, and I think it may turn out to be the right move.

    Pivoting from AMD to Micron is a huge change in mindset. While AMD is potentially overvalued, Micron is very cheap. It trades for just 3.9 times fiscal-year 2027 earnings.

    MU PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts.

    That's a very cheap price tag, and it conveys that the market thinks something is wrong with the company. However, that's far from the case.

    Sources indicate that micron operates in the memory chip industry, which has a history of being cyclical. The current artificial intelligence (AI)-driven cycle is massive and unlike anything investors have ever seen, and will eventually come to an end. The market is worried about it coming to an end sooner rather than later.

    However, memory chip companies have sold out production capacity for years in advance, and Micron's management team told investors during its latest conference call that the memory chip market conditions will be worse in 2027 and 2028 than they were in 2026, meaning that prices will stay elevated, boosting Micron's stock.

    According to recent reports, this is likely why Tepper invested in Micron, as he sees upside when the rest of the market is bearish. Tepper is so bullish on the stock that he has made it his largest position, accounting for about 17.5% of his portfolio. That's a very concentrated position, but if Micron can see its valuation expand to more reasonable levels, Tepper will make a huge profit from his Micron shares.

    If you're an AMD shareholder, I think the right move is to follow in Tepper's footsteps and roll the profits from that investment into Micron, as it could be due for a huge run over the next few years as the market realizes that the AI buildup isn't slowing down anytime soon.
